chapters.title: Kickoff and Q3 results
chapters.gist: Sofia sets the agenda and walks through Q3: on-time delivery up to 93.8% from 90.1%, fuel cost down 8% across 180 vans in three metros; Jordan agrees the numbers are good but flags the Sep 24 outage as the main topic.

chapters.title: The Sep 24 outage and service credit
chapters.gist: Jordan and Aisha describe the impact of the Sep 24 ETA outage, about 1,100 customers with wrong windows and a flooded support line; Jordan's main complaint is that the status page lagged 26 minutes and they heard from drivers first. Asher owns it, Sofia offers a 10% credit on one month, and Jordan accepts.

chapters.title: Live ETA sharing and the Q4 roadmap
chapters.gist: Jordan presses on live ETA sharing, which he first asked for in June; Asher explains it is not built, needs about five engineer-weeks, and competes with driver onboarding work, and commits to send the Q4 roadmap with a specific live ETA date by Oct 9.

chapters.title: Driver app onboarding pain for seasonal drivers
chapters.gist: Aisha details why new seasonal drivers struggle with the driver app: email-and-code login, location permissions that break tracking, and no way to practice before a live route. Asher connects it to Priya's onboarding redesign and asks for Brightside drivers to test it; Jordan notes the tension with live ETA for Q4 capacity.

chapters.title: Sacramento expansion, renewal and next steps
chapters.gist: Jordan says Brightside plans a fourth metro in Sacramento with about 60 more vans in Q1, but awarding it to Tandem depends on reliability and live ETA; Sofia proposes folding Sacramento into the Jan 31 renewal, and the call closes with a recap of commitments and clear stakes.

turns.t: Hi, hey Jordan, can you hear me okay? I think Teams just did the thing where it switched my mic to the laptop again.
Yeah, I can hear you. You're a little quiet but it's fine.
Okay, hang on, let me — is that better?
Better, yeah.
Great. So Asher's on from our side, and I saw Aisha accepted, so she should be joining.
Hey Jordan. Good to see you.
Hey Asher. Yeah, Aisha's coming, she was out on the floor at the depot when I left, so give her a minute.
No problem at all. While we wait, did you guys survive the heat last week? I saw it was like a hundred and four out there on Thursday.

Oh, don't. We had two vans where the reefer units just gave up, middle of the afternoon, full of dairy. So that was a fun day. Nothing to do with you guys, to be clear, that one's on our maintenance schedule. But yeah. It's been a month.
Oof. Yeah, I believe it.
Hi, sorry, sorry. I'm here. I was literally walking out of the loading bay.

Hey Aisha, perfect timing, we were just talking about your reefer units, so. Okay. So I'll keep the intro short. I put an agenda in the invite, but roughly, I want to start with the Q3 numbers because some of them are genuinely good and I want you to have them. Then the twenty-fourth, which I know is the big one, and Asher's here partly for that. Then roadmap, including live ETA sharing. Then Aisha, I'd love to hear from you about the driver side. And then we save time at the end for Sacramento and for the renewal. Does that work? Anything you'd add?
That works. I'll just be upfront, the twenty-fourth is the thing I most want to talk about, so let's not rush through it to get to the slides.
Totally fair. We won't. I'll go quick on the numbers and then we'll give that the time it needs.
Okay.

So, Q3. On-time delivery across all three metros was ninety-three point eight percent for the quarter. In Q2 it was ninety point one. So that's a bit over three and a half points, which, at your volume, that's a lot of deliveries that landed inside the window that didn't before. Fuel cost is down eight percent quarter over quarter. And that's on the same footprint, a hundred and eighty vans, three metros, so it's not like we got there by adding capacity. Most of that is the stop sequencing changes we made in July, and the time window tightening Aisha's team did on the evening slots. I'll share the deck after, it's got the per-metro breakdown.
Is the eight percent raw fuel spend, or is that normalized? Because diesel was up in August, so if it's raw I'd actually be surprised.

Good question. It's — so it's fuel spend per route, uh, no, sorry, let me correct that. It's gallons per route, so it's volume, not dollars. So diesel prices don't touch it. In dollars it's a bit smaller because of August, I think it's closer to six, but I'll put both numbers in the deck so you're not guessing.
Yeah, put both. My CFO will ask the exact same thing.

Will do. And the other one I wanted to call out, because it doesn't show up in on-time, is re-optimization. Your dispatchers re-ran routes mid-day about four times as often in Q3 as in Q2. Which, to me, says they actually trust it now. Back in the spring they were doing a lot of it by hand, dragging stops around.

Yeah, that's true. That's mostly because we stopped fighting it. The on-time thing matches what I'm seeing too, for what it's worth. The Tuesday and Wednesday routes in particular, those used to be our worst days and they're fine now. Where it's still rough is the north depot. The routes look good on paper and then the driver sits at a loading dock for twenty-five minutes behind a pallet truck and the whole thing slides.
Is north in the ninety-three eight, or is that dragging it down?
It's in it. North is the lowest of the three, it's around ninety-one, so the other two are carrying it a bit. It's on the second slide.

Yeah, and that's — dock wait time is honestly the hardest thing for the ETA model right now. Kenji, who runs our ML ETA work, his model's error is down from about six minutes to about four point three on average, which is a big improvement, but dense urban stops and dock waits are exactly where it still misses. That's a lot of what Routing v3 is going after. That's the new engine. It's in beta with six fleets right now, GA is November seventeenth, and the beta fleets are seeing about eleven percent fewer miles and on-time going from around ninety-one to ninety-four and a half.
And we're not in that beta.

You're not, no. We kept the beta to smaller fleets on purpose, so if something broke it didn't break a hundred and eighty vans. But you'd be one of the first we move after GA, and I'd want Aisha's north depot to be the first place we turn it on, honestly, because that's where it should help most.
I'd take that.

Okay. Look, the numbers are good. I'm not going to pretend they're not. When I showed our CEO the on-time number he was happy, for about a week. And then the twenty-fourth happened, and that's what he remembers now. So.
Yeah. Understood. Let's go there.

So I'll tell you how that morning looked from our side, because I'm not sure you have the full picture. It started a little after seven our time, which is the first wave, that's the busiest hour we have. Drivers are loaded and out. And the ETAs just stopped moving. The app kept showing times, so nobody on our side knew anything was wrong, the times just weren't real. And our customer texts go out off those ETAs. So about eleven hundred customers got a delivery window that was wrong. Some by twenty minutes, some by over an hour. And grocery customers, you know, they're waiting at home for frozen stuff, they planned their morning around it. Our support line got absolutely hammered. We normally take maybe two-fifty calls on a weekday. That day we took something like nine hundred.
Mm.

And honestly, the outage itself, things break, I've run operations long enough, I get it. The part that I'm actually upset about is that we heard about it from our drivers. Not from you. A driver called Aisha and said the app was frozen, and that was the first anyone at Brightside knew. And then your status page said everything was green for, what was it, twenty-six minutes? I had my team refreshing it. Green. So I'm on the phone with my support lead telling her I don't know what's happening, and your page is telling me nothing is happening.

Yeah, it was — so the drivers have a group chat, and by like seven-twenty it was just everyone posting screenshots. Is anyone else's app stuck. Restarting phones. A couple of them started calling customers directly from their personal phones to give them a real time, which, I appreciate the hustle, but we really don't want drivers doing that while they're driving. And I couldn't tell them anything because I didn't know anything. I ended up telling everyone to ignore the app times and just run the stop order, which, that's basically going back to paper.

And then the comps. We comped delivery fees on, I want to say three hundred-something orders, where the window was off by more than an hour or the frozen stuff was soft when it got there. That's our cost, we made that call, I'm not asking you to eat it line by line. But I want you to understand it wasn't just an annoying morning.
No, that's — thank you for laying it out. That's more detail than I had, honestly. I knew it was bad, I didn't know about the comps.

Yeah. So first, I'm sorry. And I want to be specific about what I'm sorry for, because I think you're right about where the real failure was. The ETA service went down for forty-seven minutes, and that's bad, but the part that's genuinely on us and shouldn't have happened is that you found out from your drivers, and that our status page sat green for twenty-six minutes. That's not a technical limitation. Our status page is updated by hand right now, and during the incident the person running it was also the person debugging it. That's a process failure and it's mine to fix, not your problem to work around.
Okay. I appreciate you saying that.

And just quickly on what actually happened, so you've got it. We had a failover in one of our Redis clusters, that's a cache that sits behind the ETA service. That on its own should be a blip. But our dispatch workers started retrying all at once, no backoff, no randomness, so they basically hammered the ETA service until it fell over. And the cached ETAs your drivers were seeing were stale, and nothing in the app told them that. We did a full retro last Friday, the day after. Coming out of it, the workers get proper retry budgets with jitter, the ETA service gets a circuit breaker so it degrades instead of collapsing, and the status page gets updated automatically from our alerts, so a human doesn't have to remember to do it in the middle of a fire. We're also adding a staleness flag, so if an ETA is old, the driver app says so instead of showing a confident wrong number.
Why did it take you that long to even know? Twenty-six minutes, I mean, my drivers knew in five.

Honestly, our alerting was too lenient. The threshold was set so it only paged once errors had been high for a sustained window, which is meant to stop false alarms at three in the morning, but it meant our on-call engineer got paged about six minutes after it started instead of right away. And then it took a while to figure out that the cache failover was the cause and not the symptom. Those thresholds are being tightened this week. That's not an excuse, it's just the honest answer to why.

The staleness flag, yeah. That's actually the one I care about most for the drivers. If it had just said ETA updating or something, they would have known. They wouldn't have been restarting phones for twenty minutes.

Fine. What I'd add is, the status page being automatic is good, but I don't want to be checking a status page. If something hits our fleet, I want a call or a text. Me and Aisha. Before our drivers know.

Yes. That's — I'm writing a customer comms runbook right now, that came out of the retro too, and part of it is exactly that. For accounts like yours there's a named contact list and a pre-approved message we send within, the target is fifteen minutes. I'll add you and Aisha by text, today. And I'll send you the written incident report by Friday, so you have something to hand to your CEO that isn't just me saying sorry on a call.
That would help. He's going to ask me for it.

And then, look, I have to ask. We had nine hundred support calls and eleven hundred customers with bad windows. Some of those we comped. I need to go back with something. What are we talking about on a service credit?

Yeah. So I talked to our finance team before this call, so I'm not making it up on the spot. What we can do is a credit of ten percent of one month, applied to the October invoice. That's — on your current contract that's about twelve hundred dollars. I know that doesn't cover what that morning cost you. It's not meant to pretend it does. It's meant to say we take it seriously.

Yeah. I mean, honestly, I'll take it, and the money isn't really the point. Twelve hundred bucks isn't going to change anything for us. It's more that I need to show we raised it and you responded. So yes, ten percent, October invoice, fine. What actually matters is that it doesn't happen again, and if it does, I hear it from you first.
Understood. That's fair.

And I'd rather you hold us to the second part than the credit, honestly. If there's another incident and you hear about it from a driver before you hear from Sofia, that's the thing I want you to call me about.
Oh, I will.
He will.
Okay. Let's move on before I get worked up again.
So that's a good segue actually, because the next thing on the list is roadmap, and I know live ETA is the one you want to hear about.

It is. And I'll be honest with you, I'm a little frustrated about it. I asked in June. I was on a call with you, Sofia, I think it was the mid-year check-in, and I said we need a tracking link our customers can open, live driver location, live ETA. And the answer was, it's on the roadmap. And now it's the end of September and I'm asking again.
You did, yeah. That's right.

And the reason I keep pushing is our customers expect it now. They get it from every food delivery app on their phone. Our competitors in two of our metros have it. When someone gets a delivery window of nine to eleven, and it's ten-forty and nothing's showed up, they call us. If they had a link, half those calls go away. That's real money for my support team. And frankly, on the twenty-fourth, if they'd had a live link, at least they'd have seen the van moving.

Yeah. Let me give you the straight version, because I think you've gotten the soft version a couple of times and that's not fair to you. Live ETA sharing is not built. We haven't started it. We've scoped it, it's about five engineer-weeks of work, so it's not a giant project, but it's not nothing. And for Q4 it's competing directly with something else on our list, which is a redesign of the driver app onboarding, which, Aisha, I want to come back to with you, because I think it's relevant to you too. We're finalizing Q4 planning this week. Friday, actually.
Okay, but I've heard, we're figuring out Q4, before. In June it was, we're figuring out Q3.

That's fair. So here's what I'll commit to. By October ninth, so a week from Friday, I will send you the Q4 roadmap, and it'll have a date for live ETA sharing in it. A date, not a quarter. And if the honest answer is that the date is later than you want, I'll tell you that, and I'll tell you why, rather than giving you something vague and letting you find out in January.
A date. Not a range.
A date. If I can't give you one I'll tell you exactly what it depends on, but I'm planning to give you one.
Okay. I'll hold you to that.

Please do. And I'll say one more thing on it, which ties back to the outage. If we'd shipped live ETA in July and then had the twenty-fourth, your customers would have been watching a live link show them a wrong time with total confidence. So the staleness work we're doing, the flag that says this ETA is old, that actually has to land before or with live ETA. It's not a reason to delay. It's just part of doing it right.
Yeah, that's — fine, that makes sense. I don't want a link that lies to people either. That'd be worse than no link.
What does it actually look like, though? Like if I'm a customer. Do I get a text with a link, do I need to download something? Because if it's an app download, nobody's doing that for groceries.

No download. The way we've scoped it, it's a link in the text message you already send, opens in the browser, shows the van on a map once the driver's a few stops away, and a live ETA that updates. Branded as Brightside, not as us. Your customers would never see the word Tandem. And it hides the driver's exact location until they're close, for the driver's privacy, which I think Aisha's drivers would care about.
They would, yeah. Some of them would be really uncomfortable if a customer could watch them sitting on their lunch break.

But can I add one thing from the driver side? The drivers want this too. It's not just customers. Right now when someone's anxious about their order they call the store, the store calls dispatch, dispatch calls the driver. Or the customer just calls the driver directly if they got the number from a previous delivery. The drivers hate it. They're trying to find parking and their phone's ringing with where are you. A link would take a lot of that away.

That's really useful, actually. Can I quote you on that internally? Because the driver-side benefit is a part of the case that I don't think we've been making. We've been pitching it as a customer feature and a support cost thing.
Sure, quote away.
And is it just us asking for this? Because if it's just Brightside, I get that it's harder to prioritize.

No, it's not just you. I can't name names, but we've got a large prospect right now where it's a must-have, not a nice-to-have, and a couple of other customers have asked. So it's not a favor for one account. It's something we need. The question is genuinely sequencing, not whether.
Okay. Good. That's actually reassuring, weirdly. If other people are pushing too, it's more likely to happen.
It is, yeah. You're in good company on this one.

And Jordan, just so it's clear, the roadmap Asher sends on the ninth, I'll put time on the calendar right after so we can walk through it together, rather than you just getting a PDF and having to interpret it.
Sure. That's fine. Just make sure the date's actually in it.

Okay, so Aisha, that's actually a good handoff to you. Asher mentioned the driver onboarding work, and I know you've had some things you wanted to raise about the driver app. I'd love to just hear it, unfiltered.

Yeah. Okay. So, unfiltered. The app is fine once a driver knows it. My experienced drivers, honestly, they like it, they don't think about it. The problem is new drivers, and specifically seasonal drivers. We staff up every year from mid-November through New Year's, Thanksgiving is our biggest week by a mile, and this year we're bringing on about forty-five seasonal drivers across the three metros. A lot of them have never driven for a delivery company. Some of them are, you know, college kids home for the holidays, some are retirees picking up shifts. And the first day with the app is rough.
Can you walk me through where it goes wrong? Like literally step by step, if you can.

Sure. So step one is login. Right now it's an email plus a company code. Our seasonal folks don't get a Brightside email, so they use their personal one, and half of them mistype it when we set them up, or they use a different one when they log in, and then they're locked out on their first morning, standing in the depot at six a.m., and a dispatcher has to stop what they're doing to sort it out. That alone, last November, I think we had something like a dozen lockouts in the first week.
Mm-hm.

Then permissions. Especially on Android. The phone asks, do you want to allow location all the time, only while using the app, or don't allow. And a new driver doesn't know what that means, so they tap only while using, because that sounds safer. And then they switch over to make a phone call or open the camera for a proof of delivery photo, and tracking just stops, and on our dispatch screen the van looks like it's parked for twenty minutes. And then dispatch calls them to ask if they're okay. Which, again, phone ringing while driving.
Yeah, we've seen that one on a couple of other accounts too.

And then the big one is the first route is real. There's no practice. Their first ever stop in the app is a real customer with real groceries. So they don't know how to mark a stop as customer not home, they don't know how to do a substitution note, they don't know that you can swipe to see the next three stops. And they panic a little, and they slow down, and they call dispatch. The experienced drivers end up training them in the parking lot, which, that's half a day of a good driver not driving.
What about proof of delivery? Is the photo step a problem, or is that one okay?

It's okay once they find it. The problem is it's two taps deep, so new people complete the stop without the photo, and then they get flagged, and then we get a dispute from the customer three days later saying their bags never showed up and we have no photo. That's maybe a smaller thing. But it's the same pattern, it's stuff that's obvious to someone who's done two hundred routes and invisible to someone on their first.
Yeah. Okay. I'm writing that one down, I don't think it's in the redesign yet.
And they quit. That's the part that costs me. We spend money recruiting them, we do the background check, and then they have one bad morning and don't come back.

Yeah. Last year we onboarded thirty-two seasonal drivers, and I think eleven of them never finished their first route. Or quit within the first, no, sorry, it was twelve. Twelve didn't make it through the first week. Some of that is just seasonal work, people flake. But a lot of it is that first morning.

Okay, so this is really helpful, and it lines up almost exactly with what we're seeing across all our customers. Across the board, about thirty-eight percent of new drivers drop off before they complete their first route. Our goal for Q4 is to get that below fifteen. Priya, who leads design on our side, has a redesign of the onboarding flow, and the three main pieces are basically your list. Login by phone number with a text code instead of email plus company code. A short permissions primer, three screens, that explains in plain language why the app needs location all the time before the phone asks the scary question. And a practice route, so a new driver can run through five fake stops in the depot, including a customer not home and a substitution, before they ever touch a real order.
Oh, okay. Yeah. That's — honestly, if you'd asked me to write the list, that's the list.

So my ask would be, would you be open to having a few of your drivers test it with Priya? Ideally new ones. Even four or five people. She'd do it in person or over video, half an hour each, and it'd be on the prototype, so nothing touches your live routes.

Yes. Absolutely. We have an early cohort of seasonal hires starting the third week of October, before the big wave. I could probably get you four or five of them. And I'll send over what I've got from last year too, I have a spreadsheet of the support tickets and the stuff dispatchers wrote down, it's messy but it's real.
Messy and real is perfect. I'll connect you and Priya this week.

Can I just, I want to make sure I understand. Earlier you said live ETA and this onboarding work are competing for the same people in Q4. So if you do this, are you telling me you're not doing live ETA?

It's a fair question. It's not quite either-or, but it is a real trade-off, and I'd rather be honest about it than pretend we have infinite engineers. Both of them pull on the same mobile and frontend folks. We're also hiring for exactly that right now, two senior frontend engineers, but realistically those people don't help us in Q4. So what I'm working out this week is the sequencing. That's part of why I want to give you a real date on the ninth and not a fast one.
I'll be honest, I want both.
I mean, for me, in November, onboarding matters more. If I lose twelve drivers in Thanksgiving week again, a tracking link doesn't help anybody, because the groceries aren't on a van.
Noted, Aisha. Thank you.
Just saying.
No, it's genuinely useful for us to hear both of those, because they're both real. And it's good input for Friday.
Okay. Point taken. I still want both. But point taken.
So I want to make sure we have real time for the last piece. Jordan, last time we talked you mentioned Sacramento. Where are you on that?

Yeah. So, Sacramento is happening. We signed the lease on the depot two weeks ago. We're planning to launch in Q1, probably late February if construction behaves, and the plan is about sixty vans to start. Which gets us to two-forty total. And I'll be direct with you about where that sits. I'd like to run Sacramento on Tandem. It's easier for us, one system, Aisha's team already knows it, our dispatchers know it. That's the default. But I have to make that call by mid-December, because we need to train people in January, and it's contingent on two things.
Okay.

One is reliability. I need October and November to be clean. If we have another twenty-fourth, especially in Thanksgiving week, I can't go to my CEO and say let's put another sixty vans on the same platform. I just can't. And two is live ETA. Sacramento is a new market for us, we're going to be competing with people who already have tracking links, and I'm not launching a new metro without one. So if the date you send me on the ninth is, I don't know, next summer, then I have to look at whether we run Sacramento on something else. I don't want to. But I would.
That's clear. And honestly, I appreciate you telling us straight instead of us finding out in December.

I'd rather tell you now. You've been good partners for two years. The numbers this quarter are proof of that. I'm not looking for an excuse to leave. I'm telling you what I need to be able to stay and grow.
And on reliability, what do I actually tell my CEO? Like, beyond the things you listed from the retro. Because he's going to say, how do you know it won't happen again in Thanksgiving week.

Two things you can tell him. One, we're going to start deliberately failing over that cache cluster every month, in a controlled way, so we find out how the system reacts on a Tuesday afternoon that we picked, not on a busy morning that we didn't. And two, we're going to put a change freeze around Thanksgiving week, no risky deploys to the dispatch or ETA paths that week. I can't promise you nothing will ever break. Nobody honest can. But I can promise that if it does, it breaks smaller, and you hear from us first.
Okay. The freeze, I like. Put that in writing in the incident report, if you can.

I'll put it in. And Aisha, on that, it'd help us to have your Thanksgiving week volume forecast. Orders per day, and how many vans you're running per metro. If we know the peak, we can make sure we're watching the right things that week.
Yeah, I can get you that. It's usually about one point six times a normal week, but I'll get the real forecast from planning. They do it by metro.

Which ties into the renewal, so let me put that on the table. Your renewal is January thirty-first. What I'd like to propose is that we don't treat those as two separate conversations. Rather than renewing the hundred and eighty vans in January and then doing a separate expansion contract for Sacramento in February, we fold Sacramento into the renewal. One agreement, two-forty vans, with the Sacramento vans starting whenever the depot goes live. That's simpler for your procurement and it means the pricing reflects the bigger footprint from day one.
I'm open to that. What does pricing look like?

I'm not going to throw a number out on this call, because I'd rather get it right than get it fast. But I'll put together a proposal for the combined renewal, with volume pricing at two-forty vans, and I'd want to have it to you in early November, after you've seen the roadmap and the live ETA date. That way you're evaluating the whole thing at once, not a price in isolation.
That's fine. Early November works. My CFO's going to want to see the renewal number next to the Sacramento number anyway, so having them together actually helps me.

Perfect. And would you be able to send us the Sacramento timeline and the van count? Even rough. Just so we can start planning the setup, the depot geofence, the zones, that kind of thing, and not be scrambling in February.
Yeah, I can do that. I've got a launch plan doc, I'll strip out the internal stuff, the lease terms and whatever, and send you the dates and the van count. Probably next week.
That'd be great, thank you.

And on our side, if Sacramento goes ahead, I'd want to launch it on Routing v3 from day one rather than migrating later. GA is November seventeenth, so by late February it'll have a few months of mileage on it. That's something we can show you in the roadmap too.
Okay. Yeah, that makes sense. No point launching on the old thing.
And if Sacramento's on the new onboarding flow from the start, that's sixty vans' worth of brand new drivers. That would be the best test you could ask for, honestly.
That's a really good point. Yeah.

Okay, so I want to recap, because there's a lot here and I want to make sure we all walk away with the same list. On our side. I'm applying the service credit, ten percent of one month, to your October invoice. I'm adding you and Aisha to direct incident notifications by text, today. I'm sending you the written incident report by Friday, with the Thanksgiving change freeze in it. Asher is sending the Q4 roadmap with a specific date for live ETA sharing by October ninth, and I'll set up a call right after to walk through it. Asher's connecting Aisha with Priya this week for the driver testing. And I'll have a combined renewal and Sacramento proposal to you in early November. On your side, Aisha's sending the seasonal driver feedback spreadsheet and lining up four or five drivers from the October cohort, plus the Thanksgiving volume forecast. And Jordan, you're sending the Sacramento timeline and van count. Did I miss anything?
No, I think that's it. I'd just add one thing to yours, which is, if anything happens with the platform between now and then, you call me. Not the status page. You.
Me. Promise. And you've got my cell.
And mine, if Sofia's not picking up.

Okay. Look, I'll say this and then we can all go. I want this to work. I mean that. The Q3 numbers are good and Aisha's team likes the product. But between now and December, I need October to go cleanly, I need a real date for live ETA, and I need to not be surprised again. If those three things happen, I think Sacramento's an easy call.
That's really clear, and thank you for being so direct about it. It makes our job easier, honestly.
Agreed. Thanks, Jordan. Thanks, Aisha. You'll have the roadmap on the ninth.
Thanks, everyone. I'll email Priya once you intro us.
Thanks all. Talk soon.
Bye, have a good rest of your day.

general.tldr: Q3 results were strong (93.8% on-time, fuel down 8%), but the Sep 24 outage and a status page that sat green for 26 minutes put the Jan 31 renewal and a 60-van Sacramento expansion at stake. Tandem gave a 10% one-month credit, and Asher committed to a dated live ETA plan by Oct 9.

items.text: Quarterly review with Brightside's VP Ops (Jordan) and Fleet Manager (Aisha). Agenda: Q3 results, the Sep 24 outage, the roadmap including live ETA sharing, driver-side feedback, and Sacramento plus the Jan 31 renewal.
Q3 was strong: on-time delivery was 93.8%, up from 90.1% in Q2, and fuel per route fell 8% with the same 180 vans in 3 metros.
Jordan is more upset about the comms failure than about the outage itself. Brightside heard about it from its drivers first, and Tandem's status page stayed green for 26 minutes.
